lines.text: Dad, what are you actually doing to that steak?
lines.speaker: pip

lines.text: I'm cooking, Pip! Heat makes it juicy, crispy, and delicious.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Grandma always said fire is magic, but is it magic or science?
lines.speaker: pip

lines.text: It is pure physics and chemistry. Let's draw it!
lines.speaker: maya

lines.text: Cooking is transforming raw food into something edible, nourishing, and delicious.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Raw plants and meat are packed with energy, but our bodies cannot easily digest them.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: To unlock those nutrients, we have to inject energy from the outside world.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: And for thousands of years, humans have relied on one universal energy source: heat.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Heat enters our food in three distinct ways.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: First is conduction: direct contact between hot atoms.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: When a steak touches a blistering iron skillet, heat conducts straight into the surface.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Second is convection: heat carried through moving liquids or gases.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Swirling boiling water cooks pasta, and rolling hot air bakes bread in a convection oven.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Third is radiation: energy traveling as waves of light.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Glowing broiler coals radiate infrared, while a microwave uses electromagnetic waves to shake water molecules.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Once that heat enters food, a molecular revolution begins.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Raw meats and eggs are filled with tightly folded proteins.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: As the temperature climbs, heat breaks the weak bonds holding them together.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: The proteins denature and unfold like loose yarn, then tangle into a firm, juicy network.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: That is why liquid egg whites turn solid white, and raw meat firms up as it cooks.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Vegetables and grains undergo their own dramatic transformation.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Raw potatoes, beans, and rice are crammed with tight, rock-hard starch granules.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: In cold water, starch granules sit completely unchanged.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: But when hot water penetrates, the starches swell like thousands of tiny sponges.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: They burst open in a process called gelatinization, turning tough plants soft and easily digestible.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Then comes the most delicious part of all: browning.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: When surface temperatures pass two hundred and eighty degrees Fahrenheit, the Maillard reaction ignites.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Amino acids from proteins crash into simple sugars.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: They fracture and recombine into hundreds of brand new flavor compounds.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: That single reaction creates the savory crust on bread, roasted coffee, and seared steak.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Pure sugars melt and caramelize, adding rich nuttiness and deep golden color.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Cooking also acts as our first line of biological defense.
lines.speaker: june

lines.text: High temperatures destroy harmful bacteria like Salmonella and E. coli in raw food.
lines.speaker: june

lines.text: Heat also deactivates enzymes that cause fresh foods to rot and spoil.
lines.speaker: june

lines.text: And it breaks down dangerous plant toxins, like the lectins found in raw kidney beans.
lines.speaker: june

lines.text: Without heat, many staples we eat every day would actually make us sick.
lines.speaker: june

lines.text: In fact, cooking may be the single reason modern humans exist at all.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Harvard anthropologist Richard Wrangham discovered that cooking effectively pre-digests our food.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Instead of chewing raw food for six hours a day, our ancestors absorbed calories in minutes.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: That massive surge of surplus energy allowed early humans to develop smaller guts and much larger brains.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: Harnessing fire did not just feed our bodies—it literally built our minds.
lines.speaker: leo

lines.text: So here is your kitchen takeaway.
lines.speaker: maya

lines.text: Match your heat transfer method to the food: conduction for a crisp sear, convection for gentle even cooking.
lines.speaker: maya

lines.text: Control internal heat: gentle temperatures keep proteins juicy, while high surface heat builds crust and aroma.
lines.speaker: maya

lines.text: And remember that cooking is an ongoing science experiment you get to eat.
lines.speaker: maya

lines.text: Cooking is using heat energy to transform physics and chemistry into flavor, safety, and human nourishment.
lines.speaker: theo

lines.text: So fire really was humanity's first superpower!
lines.speaker: pip

lines.text: Then why is cookware made from so many different metals?
lines.speaker: pip
